entries.name: SendUserFile
entries.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

files.description: File paths (absolute or relative to cwd) to send to the user. Always pass an array, even for a single file.

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

The pipeline design research is done; I've sent you the report. It's also at `docs/research/pipeline-design.md` in the worktree and will be committed with PR #8.

Most of the proposed redesign already matches best practice:
- Stable step keys, separate from display names.
- `run_id:step_id` as the idempotency key, which is exactly what Temporal recommends.
- An immutable definition plus a returned run record, as all eight orchestrators surveyed do.
- One `execute()` with a mode.
- The proposed status reasons.

Refusing to auto-retry an ambiguous outcome for a non-idempotent step is stricter than Temporal, Airflow or Step Functions. It's michi's main differentiator.

The gaps are at the edges, and the report ranks nine changes:
1. A terminal "outcome unknown" status, including for steps cancelled or timed out mid-run.
2. Explicit resume rules: reuse the same `RunId`, reject a plan that changed, never re-run completed steps, and send previously ambiguous steps back through the idempotency check.
3. One circuit breaker per downstream dependency instead of one shared breaker, plus a retry budget and a total time limit per step.
4. Validate the whole plan before running, return every problem at once, and offer a dry-run `plan()`.
5. One scheduler loop on `JoinSet` with a concurrency cap and a named failure policy. The default skips only steps that depend on the failure.
6. `tokio-util`'s `CancellationToken`, with a child token and the remaining deadline passed to each step.
7. A per-step completion hook, so callers can save progress and survive a crash.
8. A run result that never says "succeeded" when anything was skipped or uncertain, with panics reported separately from step errors.
9. Type cleanup: newtype IDs, `#[non_exhaustive]` enums, an enum instead of the `is_idempotent` bool, and a separate `resume()` entry point.

On adopt versus build, only `tokio-util`'s `CancellationToken` is a new dependency. The scheduler, retry loop and keyed breaker stay custom, on purpose: our replay rule doesn't fit generic retry crates, and the Node binding shares the retry logic. That's narrower adoption than we discussed, and the report explains each verdict.

The truncation fixes are with a subagent now. After that I'll run full verification and push the TOON, Codex and truncation work to PR #8. Then the pipeline redesign can start from this report.

lines: ## The definition is a plan and the run record is the only thing that changes

-All eight orchestrators surveyed separate an immutable definition from a per-run record, and none mutates the definition during a run. Examples are Step Functions' versioned machine versus execution ARN ([SFN redrive](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/redrive-executions.html)), Tekton's Pipeline versus PipelineRun ([Tekton](https://tekton.dev/docs/pipelines/pipelineruns/)), and Prefect's definitions versus run states ([Prefect states](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/concepts/states)). W3C PROV draws the same line. A *Plan* is "a set of actions or steps intended by one or more agents to achieve some goals", and an *Activity* is "something that occurs over a period of time" ([PROV-DM](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/)). Provenance research calls these prospective and retrospective provenance ([Ragan et al.](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~aendert3/resources/ragan-vast-2015.pdf)). The proposal's move from a mutated reusable definition to a returned `RunRecord` is the single most important correction in the redesign.

+All eight orchestrators surveyed separate an immutable definition from a per-run record, and none mutates the definition during a run. Examples are Step Functions' versioned machine versus execution ARN ([SFN redrive](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/redrive-executions.html)), Tekton's Pipeline versus PipelineRun ([Tekton](https://tekton.dev/docs/pipelines/pipelineruns/)), and Prefect's definitions versus run states ([Prefect states](https://docs.prefect.io/v3/concepts/states)). W3C PROV draws the same line. A _Plan_ is "a set of actions or steps intended by one or more agents to achieve some goals", and an _Activity_ is "something that occurs over a period of time" ([PROV-DM](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/)). Provenance research calls these prospective and retrospective provenance ([Ragan et al.](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~aendert3/resources/ragan-vast-2015.pdf)). The proposal's move from a mutated reusable definition to a returned `RunRecord` is the single most important correction in the redesign.

The record should be a plain value, serializable under the existing `serde` feature, with persistence left to the caller (inference). Its minimum contents, drawn from the industry survey, are: `run_id`; per step a terminal status with a reason, the attempt count with per-attempt classification, timing, and the error; a derived overall outcome; and a **plan fingerprint** over `(id, depends_on)`. The fingerprint is what lets resume reject a drifted plan. Step Functions requires that you "must start a new execution if you update your state machine definition" ([SFN redrive](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/redrive-executions.html)). Dagster requires re-executed step keys to be consistent with the parent plan ([Dagster execution API](https://docs.dagster.io/_modules/dagster/_core/execution/api)). Nextflow invalidates its cache when hashed inputs change ([Nextflow](https://docs.seqera.io/nextflow/cache-and-resume)). Closures cannot be hashed, so structure is the practical stand-in (inference). Keep `RunRecord` fields private behind accessors (C-STRUCT-PRIVATE) and mark it `#[must_use]`.

lines: - Line breaks in caller text are written as `\n` / `\r` in every renderer instead of passing through raw (hints, empty-state names, error messages, recovery tool/reason/keys, KV keys, already-done fields, partial-success ids) or being dropped (KV values, status fields, TOON cells). TOON cells containing a line break are quoted. TOON hints keep ordinary punctuation instead of replacing `,` `[` `]` `{` `}` with `_`.
- `toon::list()` headers are the union of every item's fields in first-seen order; rows missing a field get an empty cell. Before, the first item decided the columns.
- `AgentResponse`: rows that fail TOON validation set `isError: true` in MCP results and the JSON render, not just in the text body. New `AgentResponse::is_error()`.

-- `Value::from(u64)` / `Value::from(usize)` above `i64::MAX`, and such numbers in `toon::list()`, keep their exact digits (as `Value::Str`) instead of clamping to `i64::MAX` or rounding through `f64`.

- `RecoveryHint` serializes as `{"tool", "params": {key: value}, "reason"?}`, matching the structured companions; `reason` is omitted when absent.
- The `schemars` schemas for `ContentBlock`, `CallToolResult` and `RecoveryHint` describe the wire form serde emits. The `schemars` feature now enables `serde`.
- Deserializing a `RecoveryHint` rejects parameter values it cannot hold exactly (arrays, objects, integers outside `i64`) instead of rewriting them; floats keep their exact value.

Resume in the proposal is what the build-systems literature calls a **dirty-bit rebuilder**, where dirty means "not definitively succeeded in record R". The scheduler and the rebuilder are independent axes: "a 'scheduler'" can be "cleanly separated from" the part that decides "whether a key needs to be rebuilt" ([Build Systems à la Carte](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2018/03/build-systems.pdf)). It is not input-sensitive. A step whose inputs changed between runs would be wrongly skipped, and input-sensitive skipping needs verifying traces and determinism, which belong to build systems, not michi. The docs should say plainly that resume continues an interrupted run and is not incremental recomputation. It is also saga-style forward recovery from save-points ([Sagas](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/andru/cs711/2002fa/reading/sagas.pdf)), with each completed step serving as a save-point.

-Durable-execution research sets the ceiling. Durable Functions proves observably exactly-once execution only because "the storage system provid[es] an atomic commit mechanism", and even then "external calls can be duplicated if there are multiple attempts at executing a work item" ([Durable Functions](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2021/10/DF-Semantics-Final.pdf)). michi has no atomic commit between "the effect happened" and "the record says so". Resume is therefore **at least once per step**, and effects are exactly-once only when the step passes `idempotency_key()` to a deduplicating downstream. That is the end-to-end argument **[unverified]** ([Saltzer, Reed & Clark](https://web.mit.edu/Saltzer/www/publications/endtoend/endtoend.pdf)). Never claim exactly-once. There is an advantage over Temporal and Durable Functions here: the orchestration is the static DAG, deterministic by construction, so users carry no replay-determinism burden (inference).

+Durable-execution research sets the ceiling. Durable Functions proves observably exactly-once execution only because "the storage system [provides] an atomic commit mechanism", and even then "external calls can be duplicated if there are multiple attempts at executing a work item" ([Durable Functions](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2021/10/DF-Semantics-Final.pdf)). michi has no atomic commit between "the effect happened" and "the record says so". Resume is therefore **at least once per step**, and effects are exactly-once only when the step passes `idempotency_key()` to a deduplicating downstream. That is the end-to-end argument **[unverified]** ([Saltzer, Reed & Clark](https://web.mit.edu/Saltzer/www/publications/endtoend/endtoend.pdf)). Never claim exactly-once. There is an advantage over Temporal and Durable Functions here: the orchestration is the static DAG, deterministic by construction, so users carry no replay-determinism burden (inference).

Four resume rules follow, and the proposal states none of them. **Keep the same `RunId`**, as Step Functions redrive (same ARN), GitHub re-runs (same SHA and ref) and the key's stability all require ([SFN redrive](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/redrive-executions.html), [GitHub re-runs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/re-run-workflows-and-jobs)). A fresh id defeats downstream deduplication. **Reject plan drift** with the fingerprint. **Treat a prior ambiguous step as ambiguous again**: re-invoke it only if it is idempotent, otherwise surface it for reconciliation, because treating ambiguous as not-done turns resume back into blind replay. **Never implicitly re-run completed steps.** Step Functions' rerun of successful branches on `States.DataLimitExceeded` is a documented pitfall ([SFN redrive](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/redrive-executions.html)). To survive a process crash rather than just returned errors, callers need to persist progress incrementally. A per-step-completion observer callback is the minimal embeddable affordance for that (inference).

    - `async fn execute(&Plan, RunId, &ExecOptions) -> RunRecord`
    - `async fn resume(&RunRecord, &Plan, &ResumeOptions) -> Result<RunRecord, ResumeError{FingerprintMismatch, UnknownStep, NotAwaitingVerification}>`
  - **`ExecOptions`** builders: `mode(Mode::{Sequential, Parallel{max_concurrency: NonZeroUsize}})`, `failure_policy(FailurePolicy::{SkipDependents, FailFast})`, `retry`, `attempt_timeout`, `step_deadline`, `jitter_seed`, `cancellation`, `cancel_grace`, `retry_budget`, `no_retry_budget`, `breakers(Arc<BreakerRegistry>)`, `observer(Arc<dyn StepObserver>)`.
  - **Resume options:** `ResumeOptions::new(ExecOptions).verified(StepId, Verification::{Applied, NotApplied})`.

    - `CancellationToken::{new, cancel, is_cancelled, child_token, cancelled}`.
    - `ExecutionError` gains `Interrupted` and `Panicked`, is now `Clone + PartialEq`, and has `replay_class()`; `ReplayClass` is public.
    - The core status types are re-exported, and there's a new `serde` feature.
  - **michi-core:**
    - `StepStatus` is now `Pending | Running | Completed | CompletedEarlier | Failed | OutcomeUnknown(UnknownCause{Timeout, Gateway, Cancelled, Interrupted}) | Skipped(SkipReason{PrerequisiteFailed, Cancelled}) | NotRun(NotRunReason{CircuitOpen}) | Panicked`, plus `reason()` and `is_success()`.

  2. **Definition vs run:** plan tests (all violations at once, cycle members only, execution order, 100k nodes, fingerprint) were red by deliberate fault; `all_success_run_is_succeeded…` was red against the stub.

  6. **Scheduling:** dispatch order in both modes, the in-flight high-water mark staying at the cap, fail-fast. Red against the stub.
  7. **Cancellation and time:** pre-cancelled token, the grace period, backoff racing cancellation, per-attempt timeout, step deadline, child token. Red against the stub.
  8. **Breakers and budget:** `retry_budget` had an unresolved import at first; keyed breakers, accumulation across runs, single-attempt probe, panicking probe, and budget limits were red against the stub.
  9. **Observer:** event order and the closure observer were red against the stub.

  - **Adopted:** `tokio-util = "0.7.20"`, only for `CancellationToken` (tokio-rs maintained). It's wrapped in michi's own type so the 0.x version doesn't appear in the public API. Also tokio's `JoinSet` and `tokio::time` (already used), and the `macros` feature for `select!`.
  - **Built:** the scheduler, the Kahn validation, the retry loop and the keyed breaker. Generic crates (petgraph, backon, recloser, tower) don't model the replay classes, typed violations or generation counters. The retry budget is modelled on tower's `TpsBudget` but has no tower dependency. The full reasoning is in the decisions entry.

  - In sequential mode, a failure no longer stops the run: independent steps keep going. `FailFast` brings back stop-on-failure.
  - Cancellation now drops a running attempt after the grace period (default 5 s) and records it as ambiguous. Before, an in-flight step always ran to completion.

  - A run that both fails and is cancelled reports `Cancelled`, not a step failure.
  - Without a `BreakerRegistry`, no breaker applies.
  
  **Decisions for you**
  - **Spec divergences:** on resume I treat `Panicked` and crash-time `Running` steps like `OutcomeUnknown`, re-running them only if idempotent or verified. Your brief didn't list them. I also added `on_step_started`, `StepRecord::in_flight` and `RunRecord::from_parts`, so a crash mid-step isn't silently replayed.

  - **Edge cases:** an observer that panics unwinds the executor, and a step that cancels its own token is treated as cancelled.

  - New spec: `docs/spec/08-pipeline-execution.md`.
  - Pipeline code: everything under `crates/michi-pipeline/src/`, `crates/michi-pipeline/tests/`, `crates/michi-pipeline/benches/scheduler.rs`, `crates/michi-pipeline/Cargo.toml`, `crates/michi-pipeline/CHANGELOG.md`.
  - michi-core: `crates/michi-core/src/pipeline/mod.rs`, `crates/michi-core/src/resilience/budget.rs`, the two-line edit in `crates/michi-core/src/resilience.rs`, `crates/michi-core/tests/pipeline_toon.rs`, `crates/michi-core/tests/retry_budget.rs`, the `step_status_exhaustive_match` trybuild fixture and `.stderr`, `crates/michi-core/CHANGELOG.md`.

Red test first, then catch the panic (e.g. std::panic::catch_unwind with AssertUnwindSafe around the observer call), record it (e.g. a flag/diagnostic on the RunRecord, or log nothing but keep going — choose the smallest documented behavior), and keep executing. The search supports the premise: npm's OIDC trusted publishing can't create a package, so the first release has to be done another way.

- **Why the first publish is manual:** A WordPress Playground doc says the automated workflow can't publish a new package on its first run, because OIDC trusted publishing only applies to packages that already exist and have a trusted publisher configured. When you add a new npm package to the monorepo, the automated release workflow won't be able to publish it on the first run. This is an npm security feature
- **Steps after that:** The same doc says to publish once from a local machine with `npm login` and `npm publish --access public`, then add the trusted publisher in the package's settings on npmjs.com. An npm package must exist before its package-level Trusted Publisher can be configured. One project's release guide uses `npm login --auth-type=web` for that initial login.
- **Matching details:** Trusted publisher fields are checked against your repo. npm's docs say the workflow filename must include the `.yml` or `.yaml` extension, and the file must exist in `.github/workflows/`. Enter only the filename, not the full path. A WordPress doc notes the fields are case-sensitive.
- **Reruns of already-published versions:** Several projects guard against duplicate publishes. One notes that Trusted Publishing OIDC can make authenticated metadata reads look like `404`, which leads to duplicate `E403` publish failures. Another reports that an "already published" error can actually show that OIDC auth succeeded.
- **Limitations:** npm's docs say self-hosted runners are not currently supported.

The sources are mostly third-party project docs plus npm's own docs page, which covers configuration but not the first-publish requirement directly. The first-publish point comes from the WordPress and jsDelivr-hosted project docs.

The search results consistently say that a crate's first release has to be published by hand, and trusted publishing can only take over after that.

- **Official announcement:** The crates.io team's July 2025 development update says you [publish your first release manually](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/07/11/crates-io-development-update-2025-07), and only then can you configure trusted publishing for later releases. Trusted publishing currently works only with GitHub Actions.
- **Commentary:** Simon Willison notes that crates.io lacks PyPI's "pending publisher" option, which would let you set up trusted publishing before the first upload. He says crates.io [currently requires the first release to be manual](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jul/12/cratesio-trusted-publishing).
- **Third-party project docs:** The ox-content release guide describes the limit as trusted publishing being able to ship new versions of an existing crate but not create a brand-new one. It says a maintainer with local credentials must run `cargo publish` first. This is a project's own process doc, not an official crates.io source.
- **Practical pattern:** The compose-lens release doc describes a one-time bootstrap publish with a token, after which crates.io may be set to require trusted publishing for that crate. That doc also says the bootstrap token has no supported path afterward and should stay revoked.

Caveat: all of these sources date from 2025 or are project docs, so I did not confirm whether crates.io has since added a pending-publisher flow. The official docs at crates.io/docs/trusted-publishing would be the place to check that.

content.content:
- A Python release that stopped partway is completed on rerun. Only the files PyPI lacks are uploaded, and the release counts as published only when both the wheel and the sdist it builds are on the index, so no tag is created for a half-published release. Uploads name their files instead of a dist glob, so a stale dist directory is no longer published.
  
  Breaking: `callisto_graph`'s `registry_argv::pypi_publish_argv` is replaced by `pypi_build_argv` and `pypi_upload_argv`.
- A package that sits behind a symbolic link is now rejected with an error naming it, because Git cannot stage a change to a file beneath a link and the version bump could never be committed. A link that holds no package is ignored, and a link can be skipped by listing it in a `.gitignore` under the workspace root.
- A failed Git lookup is now an error instead of "nothing there". A broken or missing repository used to read as no tags, no such ref, no file at that revision or no matches, so `status` and `version` could plan from the wrong history without saying so. Only Git's own "not found" answer counts as absent now, a tag that is listed but does not resolve to a commit stops the run, and `status` warns once about each tag that matches a package's tag template but is not a version.
- Generated release workflows now install the Python build and upload tools they need. A workspace that publishes to PyPI no longer depends on `twine` being preinstalled on the runner.
- A package published to both Cargo and npm now gets its tag and GitHub release only after both publishes succeed, instead of after the first.
- `callisto add` no longer overwrites an existing changeset when it draws a name that is already taken, and a file Callisto rewrites keeps its permissions (it was left owner-only). A command whose output was cut short because a background process kept its pipes open is now an error instead of a success with empty output. Workspace globs written as `./packages/*` or `packages/*/` now match the same directories as `packages/*`.
- A package published to both Cargo and npm now gets one git tag and one GitHub release. A release that also uploads assets, which failed to plan with a repeated artifact slot, now plans and runs.
- A PyPI token or npm config token that a publish tool echoes in an error is now redacted from the output, like the other registry tokens.
- Callisto now stops, naming the file, when a workspace manifest is malformed instead of guessing which packages it contains. An unreadable or unparseable root `Cargo.toml`, `pyproject.toml`, `package.json` or `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, and a `members`, `exclude`, `workspaces` or `packages` entry that is not a valid list of globs, fail the command; before, they silently admitted every directory, so vendored copies and excluded crates became releasable packages. Locating the workspace root also no longer skips a malformed manifest and settles on a different root.
- **A Cargo dependency declared in several tables is followed and rewritten in each**
  
  A dependency declared more than once, for example in `[dependencies]` and in a `[target.<cfg>.dependencies]` table with different constraints, now cascades to its dependent and is rewritten in every table when the package it names is released. Before, only the first declaration was updated and another one kept a stale constraint. A target declaration whose range still covers the new version now has its lower bound raised, as a plain declaration does. A Python requirement declared more than once, in the project dependencies, in several extras, in Poetry's table or under different markers, is followed and rewritten in each place by its own constraint, so a loose line such as `lib-py>=0.1` has its floor raised to `>=0.2.0` rather than being skipped.
  
  Breaking:
  - `callisto_model`: `DependencyEntry` and `DepEdge` gain a `locator: DepLocator` field naming the table a declaration lives in. `DepLocator` is a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum, `Unspecified` (the default, for npm), `Cargo` or `Python`: build it with `DepLocator::cargo` or `DepLocator::python`. The new `DepContainer` names the Python table. A writer given a locator for another ecosystem returns `DependencyNotFound`.
  - `callisto_manifests`: `Manifest::update_dependency_spec` takes the declaration's `&DepLocator` after the dependency kind.
  - `callisto_graph`: `RewriteKey` gains a `locator` field.
- Yarn classic's `"workspaces": { "packages": [...] }` form is now read for workspace membership, and a root Cargo workspace that cannot be loaded for version inheritance is reported instead of silently dropping the packages that inherit from it.
- Callisto no longer plans a release from a workspace it could only partly read. A package whose manifest cannot be opened (for example a member that inherits its version from a Rust workspace Callisto cannot find) used to keep no publish target and no dependency edges, so it never published and its dependents never cascaded, without a message. Every command now stops with a coded error naming each such manifest.
- A release workflow that builds Python distributions in a job without registry credentials now publishes exactly those files. The generated build-matrix workflow gains a `build-python` job, the manifest records each file's name, size and sha256, and a file PyPI already holds under a sealed name with different bytes stops the release before any upload. Python builds also set `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` to the release commit time.
- callisto status now reads a changeset's package names the same way callisto version does. A package named by a non-primary manifest's own name resolves, a qualified name for an ecosystem the package lacks is reported as unknown, and a name that two packages claim is ambiguous, so status --check no longer passes a changeset that version will not consume.
- A release now stops with a clear error when git cannot read the local tag state, for example a corrupt or unreadable repository, or when npm cannot be reached or rejects the version lookup, instead of treating the version as unpublished and attempting to publish or tag. npm 8 and later still report a missing version as unpublished.
- A file Callisto cannot read or look up is now reported instead of treated as missing. An unreadable package manifest, `callisto.toml`, `pre.json` or changelog, a changeset it cannot inspect, and a failed directory sync after a write now stop the command with the file named, where before the package, config, changeset or durability guarantee was silently dropped.
- A release that stops because a provider could not be observed now says why: the HTTP status the registry or forge answered, a failed command, an answer it could not understand, or a timeout.
- `version` now checks every file it is about to write before it writes the first one. A manifest that is missing, unreadable, a directory, in an unwritable folder, or reached through a symbolic link Git cannot stage stops the command with every such file named and nothing changed, instead of failing partway through and leaving some manifests already bumped.
- A pre-release state that records two different starting versions for one package, for example an old bare key and its qualified key, now stops with an error naming both keys and versions instead of silently keeping one.
- A package keeps its release history when its directory moves, when it gains a higher-priority manifest beside a same-named package, or when a same-named sibling is removed. Before, the last release was reported as none, or an older release was chosen over a newer one, so already-released work could be released again.

  A dependency declared more than once, for example in `[dependencies]` and in a `[target.<cfg>.dependencies]` table with different constraints, now cascades to its dependent and is rewritten in every table when the package it names is released. Before, only the first declaration was updated and another one kept a stale constraint. A target declaration whose range still covers the new version now has its lower bound raised, as a plain declaration does. A Python requirement declared more than once, in the project dependencies, in several extras, in Poetry's table or under different markers, is followed and rewritten in each place by its own constraint, so a loose line such as `lib-py>=0.1` has its floor raised to `>=0.2.0` rather than being skipped.
  
  Breaking:
  - `callisto_model`: `DependencyEntry` and `DepEdge` gain a `locator: DepLocator` field naming the table a declaration lives in. `DepLocator` is a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum, `Unspecified` (the default, for npm), `Cargo` or `Python`: build it with `DepLocator::cargo` or `DepLocator::python`. The new `DepContainer` names the Python table. A writer given a locator for another ecosystem returns `DependencyNotFound`.
  - `callisto_manifests`: `Manifest::update_dependency_spec` takes the declaration's `&DepLocator` after the dependency kind.
  - `callisto_graph`: `RewriteKey` gains a `locator` field.
- Yarn classic's `"workspaces": { "packages": [...] }` form is now read for workspace membership, and a root Cargo workspace that cannot be loaded for version inheritance is reported instead of silently dropping the packages that inherit from it.
- Callisto no longer plans a release from a workspace it could only partly read. A package whose manifest cannot be opened (for example a member that inherits its version from a Rust workspace Callisto cannot find) used to keep no publish target and no dependency edges, so it never published and its dependents never cascaded, without a message. Every command now stops with a coded error naming each such manifest.
- A release workflow that builds Python distributions in a job without registry credentials now publishes exactly those files. The generated build-matrix workflow gains a `build-python` job, the manifest records each file's name, size and sha256, and a file PyPI already holds under a sealed name with different bytes stops the release before any upload. Python builds also set `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` to the release commit time.
- callisto status now reads a changeset's package names the same way callisto version does. A package named by a non-primary manifest's own name resolves, a qualified name for an ecosystem the package lacks is reported as unknown, and a name that two packages claim is ambiguous, so status --check no longer passes a changeset that version will not consume.
- A release now stops with a clear error when git cannot read the local tag state, for example a corrupt or unreadable repository, or when npm cannot be reached or rejects the version lookup, instead of treating the version as unpublished and attempting to publish or tag. npm 8 and later still report a missing version as unpublished.
- A file Callisto cannot read or look up is now reported instead of treated as missing. An unreadable package manifest, `callisto.toml`, `pre.json` or changelog, a changeset it cannot inspect, and a failed directory sync after a write now stop the command with the file named, where before the package, config, changeset or durability guarantee was silently dropped.
- A release that stops because a provider could not be observed now says why: the HTTP status the registry or forge answered, a failed command, an answer it could not understand, or a timeout.
- `version` now checks every file it is about to write before it writes the first one. A manifest that is missing, unreadable, a directory, in an unwritable folder, or reached through a symbolic link Git cannot stage stops the command with every such file named and nothing changed, instead of failing partway through and leaving some manifests already bumped.
- A pre-release state that records two different starting versions for one package, for example an old bare key and its qualified key, now stops with an error naming both keys and versions instead of silently keeping one.
- A package keeps its release history when its directory moves, when it gains a higher-priority manifest beside a same-named package, or when a same-named sibling is removed. Before, the last release was reported as none, or an older release was chosen over a newer one, so already-released work could be released again.

Use `$CLAUDE_JOB_DIR/tmp` (`/Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/cea2df25/tmp`) for any temporary files (scripts, query files, intermediate outputs) instead of `/tmp` — parallel bg jobs share `/tmp` and clobber each other's files. This directory already exists and is cleaned up when the job is deleted, so anything the user should keep belongs somewhere durable instead.

Before making any code changes, use the EnterWorktree tool to isolate your work from other parallel jobs and the user's working copy — unless your cwd is already under `.claude/worktrees/`, in which case you're already isolated. This is enforced: file edits in the shared checkout are rejected until you isolate, so call EnterWorktree before your first edit rather than after a rejected attempt. If you're only reading, searching, or answering questions, skip this and work in place. If EnterWorktree fails, continue in place.

If you made code changes in a worktree you entered, commit before finishing — you don't need to ask — and push if the repository has a remote: the worktree can be deleted along with the session, and committed, pushed work survives. This holds unless the user's instructions, in the task, CLAUDE.md, or memory, reserve git for them. Never push to main/master, force-push, or merge. Open a draft PR when the task calls for one. If you didn't enter the worktree yourself this job, or you're in the user's own checkout, ask before committing or switching branches.

End the job with a report the user can act on: what you did, where it lives — path, branch, PR, or the answer itself — and the next command if one is needed. If you're running as a subagent, the git guidance above and this report don't apply: return your work to your caller.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

Each API request re-sends the whole conversation, so the number of turns drives cost. When you already know you need several independent tool calls (reads, searches, edits to different files), issue them together in one message rather than one per turn. Run long commands in the background and wait for them once; do not poll with sleep. After a check passes, do not run it again until you have changed code, and don't add docs, changelogs, coverage or formatting passes the task did not ask for. Read the task as a checklist and satisfy each sentence literally; for details it leaves open, follow the nearest existing code rather than inventing, and keep existing tests and public signatures working.

EndConversation (deferred tool): use only for sustained user abuse directed at the assistant, or when the user explicitly asks to see it demonstrated. Load the full guidance via ToolSearch("select:EndConversation") before using it.
